```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
import json, pathlib
import pandas as pd

vfile = json.loads(pathlib.Path("../data/vintages.json").read_text())
vintages = vfile["vintages"]
concept_doi = vfile["concept_doi"]
n_vintages = len(vintages)
n_releases = sum(len(v["releases"]) for v in vintages.values())

manifests = {
    p.stem: json.loads(p.read_text())
    for p in pathlib.Path("../manifests").glob("*.json")
}
latest = manifests["2026-08-24"]
topic_rows = {f["topic"]: f["rows"] for f in latest["files"]
              if f.get("format") == "csv.gz"}
total_rows = sum(topic_rows.values())
csv_mb = sum(f["bytes"] for f in latest["files"] if f.get("format") == "csv.gz") / 1e6
parquet_mb = sum(f["bytes"] for f in latest["files"] if f.get("format") == "parquet") / 1e6

def fmt(n):
    return f"{n:,}"
```

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

State Cancer Profiles (statecancerprofiles.cancer.gov), maintained by the
National Cancer Institute with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention,
is a widely used source of county- and state-level cancer statistics in the
United States. The site offers no API, no bulk download, and no archive of
prior estimates: its sole machine-readable export returns one statistical
stratum per HTTP request, and when the underlying data are updated the
previous estimates are overwritten and become unrecoverable. This resource
provides the complete national county- and state-level extract of all four
State Cancer Profiles data topics — incidence, mortality, screening and risk
factors, and demographics — as typed, analysis-ready files with the
stratifying dimensions as columns, published under pinned, citable version
DOIs on Zenodo (concept DOI `{python} concept_doi`). One version DOI is
minted per distinct upstream data *vintage*; three vintages have been
captured to date, and at each observed vintage boundary roughly 98% of
estimate values changed, so vintage identity materially affects downstream
analysis. From the 2026-08-24 release forward, cells that the upstream site
suppresses are retained as typed nulls with an explicit suppression-reason
column. Capture is automated on a monthly cadence, and each future upstream
revision will be preserved as a new vintage.

# Background & Summary

State Cancer Profiles (SCP; <https://statecancerprofiles.cancer.gov>) is a
joint National Cancer Institute and Centers for Disease Control and
Prevention website that publishes cancer incidence, mortality, screening and
risk-factor, and demographic estimates for United States counties, states,
and the nation. County-level statistics of this kind underpin a substantial
share of cancer control practice and research. NCI-designated cancer centers
are required to characterize and serve defined catchment areas, and SCP is a
primary source for the geographic surveillance tools built for that purpose
[@burus2023cancerinfocus; @sonawane2024dashboards; @spees2024chana]; one such
tool has been adopted by 35 institutions, including 26 NCI-designated centers
[@burus2025cifimpact]. Published studies draw county-level SCP estimates for
questions of geographic access to oncology care
[@shalowitz2015geographic; @zhang2024oncologydensity; @crowley2026oncologists],
environmental and behavioral exposure correlates of cancer burden
[@joseph2022pesticides; @wei2025tanning], community-level determinants of
screening and mortality [@drake2025community], and incidence in
non-metropolitan counties [@jacobson2026pediatric]. All of these uses share a
dependency: the analysis dataset is whatever the SCP website served on the
day it was queried.

Obtaining these data in bulk is not supported. As of 23 August 2026, the SCP
website provided no public API and no bulk-download facility. Its
documentation describes per-table CSV export as the available method for
obtaining data, and the site's sole machine-readable export returns a single
statistical *stratum* — one cancer site × race/ethnicity × sex × age × stage
× area-type combination, covering all areas at once — per HTTP request.
Assembling one complete national county- and state-level extract required
18,852 such requests. <!-- chunk-needed: request count from
scrape_catalog.jsonl of the deposited release -->

A second limitation is temporal. NCI periodically replaces the estimates — a
new SEER/NPCR data submission, revised population denominators, a shifted
five-year window — and the site serves only the current values. We refer to
one such edition of the estimates as a **vintage**: the complete set of
values the site served during some period, bounded by the upstream
replacement. The term follows the real-time-data literature in economics,
where a data vintage is a statistical series as it existed on a given date
and where the choice of vintage is known to change analytic conclusions
[@croushore2001realtime; @croushore2003vintage]. Cancer surveillance exhibits
the same phenomenon: reporting delay and reporting error revise incidence
rates for years after first publication, by enough to change the direction of
fitted trends [@clegg2002reportingdelay; @das2008completeness]. At each
vintage boundary observed in this archive, approximately 98% of previously
published estimate values changed (Technical Validation, @fig-vintages).
No archive of superseded SCP estimates has existed: the Internet Archive's
Wayback Machine holds 35,642 pre-2023 captures of SCP CSV exports, but these
collapse to a few hundred distinct strata — under 1.3% coverage of any single
vintage, too sparse for reconstruction — while documenting eleven distinct
pre-2023 incidence data windows, each overwritten and unretrievable today. An
analysis built on SCP therefore cannot be reproduced from source after the
next upstream refresh, and the estimates that informed a past decision cannot
be re-examined.

Prior software does not close either gap. `cancerprof`
[@getwilds_cancerprof] wraps SCP's per-query CSV export in R; it was
submitted to rOpenSci software peer review, the review closed without
acceptance, and the package was never published on CRAN. It issues one live
request per stratum, does not record which vintage the numbers came from, and
caches nothing, so repeated runs of the same script can return different
values without any indication of change. An earlier R client was abandoned in
2017 [@silentspring_rscp]. A public repository associated with the Cancer
InFocus project contains an unpublished national SCP sweep feeding a
dashboard pipeline, with no release, no registry entry, and no DOI
[@ciodata_ciftools]. The demand for bulk access is nonetheless visible in the
workarounds: at least three CRAN packages ship hand-frozen, single-window SCP
slices as example data
[@sarkar_latticeextra; @pearson_seermapper; @otto_spgarch], and the one
SCP-derived deposit we located in a generalist data repository is a
single-site, single-window analysis slice [@acharjee2020airquality]. To our
knowledge, no complete SCP extract has previously been published as a
versioned, citable dataset.

This resource addresses both gaps (@fig-workflow). A scraper enumerates the
site's own query vocabulary, issues one request per stratum, and publishes
the complete national county- and state-level extract of all four data topics
as typed CSV and Parquet files in which the stratifying dimensions appear as
decoded label columns. Dated captures are published as GitHub releases on a
monthly cadence; distinct vintages are identified by content comparison, and
each receives a Zenodo version DOI under a single concept DOI, following
FAIR-oriented dataset-versioning practice
[@klump2021versioning; @gonzalezcebrian2024versioning]. The design follows
published descriptors of re-extracted public and governmental data
[@hasell2020testing; @xu2020covidcases; @ocagli2024jecfa; @vanheusden2025foia;
@karnik2025offsets; @zhang2025adtransparency]. The archive is complementary
to live query clients such as `cancerprof`: a client retrieves the current
estimates, whereas the archive preserves each superseded set of estimates
together with the releases that captured it — something a live client cannot
do once the source has been overwritten. Three vintages have been captured
across `{python} n_releases` releases to date. Vintage boundaries are known
only to within the interval between successive captures, and vintages
replaced before capture began in 2024 were not archived; the resource is
accordingly a prospective record.

![Architecture of the archive. Upper row: monthly capture — one request per
statistical stratum against the four State Cancer Profiles report endpoints,
with the query vocabulary discovered from the live site, content-based
parsing, and suppression decoding into typed nulls with a reason column.
Lower row: publication — immutable dated GitHub releases with checksum
manifests; releases are grouped into vintages by content hash, and each new
vintage receives a Zenodo version DOI under the data concept DOI. Left:
the upstream revision cycle that motivates the archive — estimates are

# Methods

The pipeline converts upstream report pages into typed tables in which every
cell of the queried stratum space is accounted for: published values, three
classes of withheld values, and combinations the site does not publish are
each represented distinctly. From the 2026-08-24 release forward, cells that
SCP suppresses are retained as rows with typed null rates and an explicit
`suppression_reason` column distinguishing small-count suppression from
state-law withholding. Earlier releases (2024-08-02 through 2026-06-01)
predate this behavior and omit suppressed rows entirely; the scope of every
claim in this section is stated accordingly.

## Source and extraction unit

SCP serves four query-driven report endpoints: incidence
(`incidencerates/`), mortality (`deathrates/`), screening and risk factors
(`risk/`), and demographics (`demographics/`). Appending `output=1` to a
report URL — the same URL the site's own "Export Data" link emits — returns
the report as CSV. One request fixes one stratum and returns all areas for
it; requesting `stateFIPS=00` with `areatype=county` returns every US county
plus the national aggregate in a single response, so geography is not an
iteration axis. The scraper iterates the cartesian product of the
stratifying dimensions per endpoint: cancer site × age × sex ×
race/ethnicity × stage × area-type for incidence, the same minus stage for
mortality (stage is not a mortality dimension upstream; see Technical
Validation), topic × risk factor × race/ethnicity × sex × state for
screening and risk factors, and area-type × topic × measure ×
race/ethnicity × sex × age for demographics.

## Query vocabulary and the scrape catalog

The query vocabulary — the valid codes for every dimension — is not
hardcoded. It is discovered at run time from the site's own HTML select
elements and JavaScript definition files, so upstream additions (a new
cancer site, a new race/ethnicity category) enter the next scrape without a
code change. Because most of the cartesian product corresponds to
combinations the site does not publish, the scraper maintains a *scrape
catalog*: an append-only record of every query combination that has ever
returned data, with row counts and first/last-seen dates. Monthly runs
iterate only the catalog; a full cartesian re-discovery runs quarterly and
whenever manually invoked. The catalog doubles as a regression oracle: a
combination that returned data at the previous release and returns nothing
now is treated as a scrape failure, not as newly dead space, and fails the
run. Requests are issued through a bounded thread pool with exponential
backoff on transport errors and server errors; failures are counted and
reported, never silently discarded.

## Payload parsing

Each response is a report, not a clean data file: a title block, the data
rows, and a footnote block, separated by blank lines. The parser locates the
data block by content — it scans for the header line carrying the FIPS or
HSA-code field — rather than by fixed line offsets, and reads column names
from the header rather than by position. The distinction has practical
consequences: SCP added a Rural-Urban Continuum Codes column to county
reports in 2023, which broke position-based parsing in `cancerprof` for
three of its four topics at county level [@getwilds_cancerprof] but passed
through this parser without incident. Everything outside the data block is
preserved verbatim in per-endpoint `notes_<endpoint>.txt` files: the data
windows, source registries, suppression-rule text, and data-submission year
that constitute the extract's provenance.

## Suppression decoding

SCP withholds a cell for two documented reasons: counts below 16 in an
area-sex-race category ("data has been suppressed to ensure confidentiality
and stability of rate estimates"), and state legislation prohibiting release
of county-level data. Suppression of this kind is standard practice in
federal health statistics [@klein2002suppression; @parker2017proportions;
@talih2023ratesstandards], and its downstream analytic cost is well
documented in the small-area disparities literature
[@santoslozada2020dp; @krieger2021dp; @li2023dpmapping]. In SCP's export the
two cases appear as an asterisk or a footnote marker inside otherwise
numeric columns. The scraper decodes them before numeric coercion: the row
is kept, the rate columns become typed nulls, and `suppression_reason` is
set to `suppressed_small_count` or `withheld_state_law`. A user can
therefore distinguish "suppressed for small counts", "legally withheld", and
"combination never published" — three states that are indistinguishable in
an extract that drops non-numeric rows, as this scraper's own releases did
before 2026-08-24.

## Vintage identification

Release artifacts are assigned to vintages by content, not by date: each
topic file is hashed (SHA-256) after dropping the single scrape-time-varying
column (`_extracted_at`), and releases sharing content hashes captured the
same upstream data. Vintage identity is keyed on the registry-observed
incidence and mortality topics only; the screening/risk-factor and
demographics topics are modelled or survey products that refresh on their
own cadence (Usage Notes). Candidate boundaries are confirmed by
decomposing each between-release difference into new query strata versus
changed values on strata common to both releases: a scope expansion of the
scraper adds strata but changes no common values, whereas an upstream
revision changes nearly all of them (Technical Validation). When the
scraper's own output format changes — as at the 2026-08-24 hardening —
content hashes no longer compare across the format change, and vintage
continuity is instead established by a value-level comparison on common
strata.

## Harmonized view

Alongside the immutable per-release files, the pipeline derives a
harmonized cross-vintage view. Harmonization decisions — label crosswalks,
column renames, the reclassification of county rows mislabelled by an
upstream quirk — are recorded as data in a checked-in crosswalk file, not
hardcoded, and the transformation enforces strict accounting: harmonized
rows plus dropped rows must equal original rows, and any imbalance fails the
build. Published release bytes are never regenerated or edited; corrections
are new releases.

## Archiving and versioning

A scheduled GitHub Actions workflow scrapes monthly, validates against the
catalog, writes a manifest of SHA-256 checksums, row counts, and byte sizes
for every artifact, and publishes a dated GitHub release. When the manifest
identifies a new vintage, the same code path mints a new Zenodo version on
the data concept DOI. Each Zenodo version deposits the *best* capture of its
vintage (the most complete release, which is not always the first), sets the
publication date to the *first* capture, and lists every GitHub release tag
that captured the vintage in its related identifiers, so the deposit
reflects both the completeness and the true chronology of capture. Code and
data are archived under separate Zenodo concepts; the data concept
(`{python} concept_doi`) is the citable identity of this resource.

# Data Records

The archive is deposited on Zenodo under concept DOI
[10.5281/zenodo.11098814](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.11098814), which
always resolves to the newest vintage. Each distinct vintage carries its own
version DOI (@tbl-vintages).

```{python}
#| output: asis
print("| Vintage | DOI | Releases capturing it | First captured | Best capture |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|")
for vid, info in sorted(vintages.items()):
    print(f"| {vid} | {info.get('doi', 'pending')} | {len(info['releases'])} | {info['first_capture']} | {info['best_capture']} |")
print()
print(": Data vintages, their Zenodo version DOIs, and the GitHub releases "
      "that captured them. The publication date of each Zenodo version is "
      "the date of the vintage's first capture; the deposited bytes are its "
      "most complete capture. {#tbl-vintages}")
```

Each vintage deposit contains one gzipped CSV per data topic; the V3 deposit
(best capture `2026-08-24`, the first from the hardened scraper) adds a
Parquet file per topic, the per-endpoint notes files, the scrape catalog,
the query vocabulary (`select_options.json`), a manifest with per-file
SHA-256 checksums, and a rendered README with citation guidance. Earlier
vintages are CSV-only captures made before the hardening and are preserved
byte-for-byte as scraped; under the immutability rule they will not gain
Parquet or suppression columns retroactively. The `2026-08-24` release
comprises `{python} fmt(total_rows)` rows across the four topics
(incidence `{python} fmt(topic_rows['incidence'])`, mortality
`{python} fmt(topic_rows['mortality'])`, demographics
`{python} fmt(topic_rows['demographics'])`, screening and risk factors
`{python} fmt(topic_rows['risk'])`), totalling approximately
`{python} f"{csv_mb:,.0f}"` MB as gzipped CSV or
`{python} f"{parquet_mb:,.0f}"` MB as Parquet.

All four topic tables share a common shape: one row per (stratum × area).
@tbl-schema lists the columns of the incidence table, the widest of the
four, as read from the deposited Parquet file. Mortality omits
`percent_of_cases_with_late_stage` and its `stage` column is constant;
demographics and screening/risk-factor tables substitute their own measure
columns (population characteristics and modelled prevalence estimates with
confidence intervals, respectively) and their own topic/measure dimension
columns, but carry the same geographic keys, provenance columns, and
decoded stratifier labels.


@fig-maps illustrates the county-level content of a single vintage: the
age-adjusted all-sites incidence rate, and the cell status of one finer
stratum in which suppression becomes visible.

```{python}
#| label: fig-maps
#| fig-cap: >
#|   County-level content of vintage V3 (release 2026-08-24). (a)
#|   Age-adjusted incidence rate per 100,000, all cancer sites, all races,
#|   both sexes. Kansas publishes no county-level incidence in any vintage
#|   and appears as missing. (b) Cell status for one finer stratum (lung and
#|   bronchus, all races, both sexes): published rate, suppressed for small
#|   counts, or withheld under state law (all Kansas counties). The color
#|   scale in (a) is truncated at the 2nd and 98th percentiles. Puerto Rico
#|   is omitted from the maps; boundaries are 2010 Census counties.
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 8.4
import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Patch

gdf = gpd.read_file("data/geo/counties.geojson")[["id", "geometry"]].set_index("id")
rate = pd.read_csv("data/fig_map_rate.csv", dtype={"fips": str}).set_index("fips")
sup = pd.read_csv("data/fig_map_suppression.csv", dtype={"fips": str}).set_index("fips")
g = gdf.join(rate).join(sup)

regions = {
    "conus": (g[~g.index.str[:2].isin(["02", "15", "72"])].to_crs("EPSG:5070"),
              [0.00, 0.00, 1.00, 1.00]),
    "ak":    (g[g.index.str[:2] == "02"].to_crs("EPSG:3338"),
              [0.01, 0.02, 0.22, 0.30]),
    "hi":    (g[g.index.str[:2] == "15"].to_crs("EPSG:26904"),
              [0.25, 0.02, 0.12, 0.16]),
}

STATUS_COLORS = {"published": "#d9d9d9",
                 "suppressed_small_count": "#E69F00",
                 "withheld_state_law": "#0072B2"}
MISSING = dict(color="#f7f7f7", edgecolor="#cccccc", linewidth=0.05)
VMIN, VMAX = g["rate"].quantile([0.02, 0.98])

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(7.2, 8.4))
panels = {"a": [0.02, 0.52, 0.96, 0.45], "b": [0.02, 0.02, 0.96, 0.45]}
for key, rect in panels.items():
    px, py, pw, ph = rect
    for name, (reg, sub) in regions.items():
        sx, sy, sw, sh = sub
        ax = fig.add_axes([px + sx * pw, py + sy * ph, sw * pw, sh * ph]
                          if name != "conus" else [px, py, pw, ph])
        ax.set_axis_off()
        if key == "a":
            reg.plot(ax=ax, column="rate", cmap="Blues", rasterized=True,
                     vmin=VMIN, vmax=VMAX,
                     linewidth=0.05, edgecolor="white", missing_kwds=MISSING)
        else:
            colors = reg["status"].map(STATUS_COLORS).fillna(MISSING["color"])
            reg.plot(ax=ax, color=colors, rasterized=True,
                     linewidth=0.05, edgecolor="white")
        if name == "conus":
            ax.set_title(
                "(a) Age-adjusted incidence rate, all cancer sites" if key == "a"
                else "(b) Cell status, lung & bronchus", fontsize=11, loc="left")

sm = plt.cm.ScalarMappable(cmap="Blues", norm=plt.Normalize(VMIN, VMAX))
cax = fig.add_axes([0.60, 0.545, 0.34, 0.012])
cb = fig.colorbar(sm, cax=cax, orientation="horizontal", extend="both")
cb.set_label("rate per 100,000", fontsize=8)
cb.ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)

handles = [Patch(facecolor=STATUS_COLORS["published"], label="published"),
           Patch(facecolor=STATUS_COLORS["suppressed_small_count"],
                 label="suppressed (small counts)"),
           Patch(facecolor=STATUS_COLORS["withheld_state_law"],
                 label="withheld (state law)"),
           Patch(facecolor=MISSING["color"], edgecolor="#cccccc",
                 label="not in stratum / no data")]
fig.legend(handles=handles, loc="lower right", bbox_to_anchor=(0.98, 0.055),
           fontsize=8, frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

The complete capture history — every dated release, including the several
releases that captured each vintage — is public on GitHub
(<https://github.com/seandavi/state-cancer-profile-scraper/releases>) with
per-release manifests in the repository. Data are licensed CC-BY-4.0; the
scraper and pipeline code are MIT-licensed.

# Technical Validation

## Release integrity

Every deposited artifact is listed in a checked-in manifest with SHA-256
checksum, byte size, and row count, and the Zenodo deposits were verified
byte-identical against these manifests at publication. @tbl-release-integrity
reports per-release, per-topic row counts and content checksums for the full
capture history.

```{python}
#| output: asis
rows = []
for tag in sorted(manifests):
    m = manifests[tag]
    for f in m["files"]:
        if f.get("format") == "csv.gz":
            rows.append((m["tag"], f["topic"], fmt(f["rows"]),
                         f.get("content_sha256", f["sha256"])[:12]))
print("| Release | Topic | Rows | Content sha256 (first 12) |")
print("|---|---|---|---|")
for r in rows:
    print("| " + " | ".join(str(x) for x in r) + " |")
print()
print(": Per-release, per-topic row counts and content checksums (SHA-256 "
      "of the file after dropping the scrape-timestamp column) for all "
      "releases. Identical checksums within a column identify releases that "
      "captured the same vintage. Mortality row counts in releases before "
      "2026-08-24 include the phantom-stage duplication described in the "
      "text. {#tbl-release-integrity}")
```

Two historical releases are defective partial scrapes rather than distinct
vintages: `2025-05-01` incidence is missing exactly one query stratum
(1,322 rows) relative to its neighbours, and `2025-09-01` mortality is
missing 4 rows; both revert identically at the next release, which upstream
revisions do not do. Both are recorded as defective in the vintage
assignments and excluded from best-capture selection.

One caveat governs historical mortality counts: in releases before
`2026-08-24` the scraper iterated a stage dimension that the mortality
endpoint ignores, so historical mortality tables contain each row twice —
once labelled all-stages and once spuriously labelled late-stage. Row
counts for those releases must be halved after deduplication, and the
phantom late-stage labels discarded; the hardened scraper no longer
iterates stage for mortality.

## Vintage assignment

Within each vintage, all clean captures are byte-identical after dropping
the extraction timestamp — eleven clean V2 releases share one content hash
per topic — so the release-to-vintage grouping is not sensitive to capture
date (@fig-vintages a). At the two observed vintage boundaries,
decomposition into new versus common strata shows the signature of upstream
revision: from V1 to V2, 98.3% of incidence values changed on 902,728
common strata-rows (98.6% of mortality on 733,172); from V2 to V3, 98.2%
changed on 981,550 (97.4% of mortality on 753,490). By contrast, the
within-V3 scraper scope expansion of `2026-05-28` added 122,041 incidence
rows while changing zero values on 1,299,615 common rows, and the
`2026-08-24` hardening changed zero values on 1.99 million common incidence
and mortality cells — confirming both as capture-scope changes, not new
vintages. <!-- chunk-needed: recompute boundary decomposition from the
deposits -->

```{python}
#| label: fig-vintages
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Capture history and revision at a vintage boundary. (a) The dated
#|   releases (points) grouped into vintages by content hash; open points
#|   are the two defective partial scrapes. (b) County-level age-adjusted
#|   all-sites incidence rates in vintage V2 (release 2026-02-01) against
#|   the same counties in vintage V3 (release 2026-08-24); the diagonal is
#|   identity. Nearly every county's published rate changed at the
#|   boundary.
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.6
import datetime
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.dates as mdates

VCOLOR = {"V1": "#0072B2", "V2": "#E69F00", "V3": "#009E73"}
fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(
    1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.6), width_ratios=[1.4, 1],
    constrained_layout=True)

for i, (vid, info) in enumerate(sorted(vintages.items())):
    dates = [datetime.date.fromisoformat(r[:10]) for r in info["releases"]]
    defect = set(info["defective_releases"])
    good = [d for r, d in zip(info["releases"], dates) if r not in defect]
    bad = [d for r, d in zip(info["releases"], dates) if r in defect]
    ax.plot([min(dates), max(dates)], [i, i], color=VCOLOR[vid],
            lw=1.2, alpha=0.5)
    ax.plot(good, [i] * len(good), "o", color=VCOLOR[vid], ms=6)
    if bad:
        ax.plot(bad, [i] * len(bad), "o", mfc="white", mec=VCOLOR[vid], ms=6)
    ax.annotate(f"{vid} — {info['doi']}",
                (min(dates), i + 0.22), fontsize=8.5, color="#333333")
ax.set_ylim(-0.5, 2.8)
ax.set_yticks([])
locator = mdates.MonthLocator(bymonth=(1, 7))
ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(locator)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.ConciseDateFormatter(locator))
ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)
ax.spines[["left", "top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.set_title("(a) Releases and vintages", fontsize=11, loc="left")

sc = pd.read_csv("data/fig_revision_scatter.csv", dtype={"fips": str})
pct_changed = (sc.rate_v2 != sc.rate_v3).mean()
bx.axline((300, 300), slope=1, color="#999999", lw=1, zorder=1)
bx.plot(sc.rate_v2, sc.rate_v3, ".", ms=2.5, alpha=0.35,
        color="#0072B2", rasterized=True, zorder=2)
bx.set_xlabel("rate per 100,000, V2 (2026-02-01)", fontsize=9)
bx.set_ylabel("rate per 100,000, V3 (2026-08-24)", fontsize=9)
bx.tick_params(labelsize=8)
bx.set_aspect("equal")
bx.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
bx.set_title("(b) All-sites county rates across the V2→V3 boundary",
             fontsize=11, loc="left")
plt.show()
```

The per-county comparison in @fig-vintages (b) is computed from the
deposited artifacts: of `{python} fmt(len(sc))` counties with a published
all-sites rate in both vintages,
`{python} f"{pct_changed:.1%}"` have different values.

Vintage boundaries are bracketed, not dated: V1→V2 is bounded by a
six-month gap in captures and V2→V3 by a missing monthly release. An
upstream vintage could in principle have come and gone inside either
window uncaptured; the archive claims only the vintages it holds.

## Coverage

Mortality coverage is essentially complete and stable (3,084–3,087
distinct counties per release, no state ever absent), consistent with its
vital-statistics origin. Incidence coverage depends on state registry
publication decisions and grows across vintages: 2,694 counties in V1,
2,933 in V2, 3,029 in V3. Kansas has no county-level incidence in any
vintage (state-level Kansas incidence appears only from `2026-05-28`),
while its county-level mortality is complete throughout — visible as the
missing block in @fig-maps (a). Indiana county incidence is absent in V1
and V2 and present, all 92 counties, from V3. Minnesota, Nevada, and
Virginia county incidence are missing only in V1.
<!-- chunk-needed: county coverage counts from the deposits -->

## Schema stability

Across all three vintages the category vocabularies are identical — 23
cancer sites, 6 race/ethnicity groups, 3 sex values, 7 age groups, 2 stage
values — and exactly one column was ever added upstream (the 2023
Rural-Urban Continuum Codes note column, at the V1→V2 boundary). Schema
stability is itself a validated property: the drift audit that produced
this finding compared column lists, inferred types, and full category
vocabularies across every release.

## Suppression census

In post-hardening files suppression is countable directly from
`suppression_reason`. In the stratum mapped in @fig-maps (b) — lung and
bronchus, all races, both sexes — the site returned 3,143 county cells:
2,797 published, 241 suppressed for small counts, and 105 (every Kansas
county) withheld under state law, matching the independent audit of the
live site. Historical releases dropped withheld rows, which is why
post-hardening captures of the same vintage are substantially larger than
earlier ones: the difference consists of retained suppressed cells and the
added state-level tier, not changed estimates.
<!-- chunk-needed: full suppression census by state and reason from the
V3 deposit -->

## Cross-topic joins

The four topics share FIPS geographic keys, and incidence × mortality
joins on `fips` plus the shared demographic dimensions are exercised in
the pipeline's tests. The demographics topic carries a race/ethnicity
vocabulary that only partially maps to the incidence/mortality one; the
harmonized view reconciles the mappable categories through the checked-in
crosswalk and leaves unmappable categories topic-local rather than forcing
a lossy alignment. <!-- chunk-needed: run the advertised join in a chunk
against the deposit before submission -->

# Usage Notes

**Vintages are not independent observations.** Incidence and mortality
estimates are five-year averages, and consecutive vintages share four of
their five years. Differencing two vintages does not estimate change over
time; it largely re-observes the same person-years after revision. Users
who need temporal contrasts should use the year windows documented in the
notes files, not vintage-over-vintage differences.

**Treatment of 2020.** SCP displays 2020 incidence but excludes it from
its trend fits owing to pandemic-era reporting disruption. Downstream
trend work must handle 2020 explicitly rather than inherit its inclusion.

**Trend statistics are software outputs.** The trend columns are Joinpoint
model outputs [@kim2000permutation; @clegg2009aapc], and Joinpoint's
defaults have changed materially over its lifetime
[@kim2022twentyyears; @kim2023modelselection]. Average annual percent
change values should not be compared across vintages without confirming
the producing software version in the notes files.

**Coverage asymmetries.** Joining incidence to mortality on FIPS silently
drops all Kansas counties from the incidence side (Kansas mortality is
complete; Kansas county incidence does not exist in any vintage). Indiana
county incidence exists only from V3, so any cross-vintage comparison
involving Indiana compares presence against absence. See Technical
Validation for the full list of V1 gaps.

**Filter on `areatype`, not `locale_type`, in pre-`2026-05-28` files.** In
those releases `locale_type` misclassifies tens of thousands of county
rows — Louisiana parishes, Alaska boroughs, independent cities, and DC —
as `other`. The harmonized view corrects this; the immutable release
bytes do not.

**Suppression semantics differ by era.** In releases from `2026-08-24`
forward, suppressed cells are present as rows with typed nulls and a
reason code. In all earlier releases, suppressed cells are simply absent,
and suppression there is recoverable only by differencing against an
expected cross-product. The archive does not un-suppress anything: it
makes suppression countable, which matters because published county
studies routinely restrict their samples to unsuppressed counties without
being able to characterize what was withheld
[@jacobson2026pediatric; @ladas2026melanoma; @kasheri2026dermatologist].

**Screening and risk-factor estimates are modelled.** They are small-area
model estimates combining BRFSS and NHIS survey data
[@raghunathan2007combining; @liu2019smallarea; @liu2025psa], not
registry-observed counts, and carry a different epistemic status from
incidence and mortality. They can change between captures because the
model was refit, not because the underlying population changed. For this
reason vintage identity is keyed on incidence and mortality only; the
Zenodo deposit for a vintage carries the newest screening/demographics
edition captured during that vintage, and earlier within-vintage editions
remain available, hash-verified, in the GitHub releases.

# Code availability {.unnumbered}

The scraper, pipeline, validation, and deposit code are available at
<https://github.com/seandavi/state-cancer-profile-scraper> under the MIT
license, and are archived per-release on Zenodo under a separate software
concept (10.5281/zenodo.13174526). Every data release records the exact
repository commit that produced it (`gh_hash.txt`), so any capture can be
traced to the code that made it. The figure and table inputs in this
article are derived from the deposited artifacts by
`manuscript/scripts/derive_figure_data.py` in the same repository.

# Data availability {.unnumbered}

All data are openly available under CC-BY-4.0. The canonical citable
deposit is Zenodo concept DOI
[10.5281/zenodo.11098814](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.11098814), with
one version DOI per vintage (@tbl-vintages). The complete dated capture
history is available as GitHub releases at
<https://github.com/seandavi/state-cancer-profile-scraper/releases>.
